title: Part 2: Privilege, conversion and lifecycle
say: Welcome to Part 2 of the implementation series for non-person identity. That means every identity that isn't a person, from an old service account to an AI agent. Part 1 listed every one of them, gave each an owner and a sponsor, decided where each one goes, and set the credential rules. Part 2 covers the last three gates. First, cutting privilege. Then converting each identity to its target, with a parallel run. Then running the lifecycle, from an owner change to a clean decommission. After that come SQL Server and AI agents, and finally the evidence and the rollback. The format is the same as Part 1. Each gate gets its steps, the workbook's lab commands with the kit's real output, the federal requirement and evidence, availability in the government clouds, an interim path, and a rollback. Design guidance is labeled, and the code is tested against fixtures, not a live tenant.

title: G4–G6 on one page: done when, validate with, rollback
say: Here are Part 2's three gates on one page. The least privilege gate is done when every high-privilege grant is justified or removed, and every Tier 1 app registered in your own tenant has a workload Conditional Access policy. The conversion gate is done when converted identities sign in without stored secrets, and the legacy accounts are disabled after a clean parallel run. The lifecycle gate is done when the owner change, orphan, review and decommission paths have all run and left records. Each gate names the read-only kit checks that prove it, and each has a rollback. Together they finish the track. Every identity has an owner, a sponsor, a reason and a target. Each one is retired, moved to a managed identity, or given a certificate or a federated credential. And none holds a password that never expires, or is left without an owner.

title: G4: cut privilege across five surfaces
say: Least privilege applies to software too, and a workload can use its access faster than any person. The guide cuts privilege in five places. First, Graph permissions. Prefer delegated permissions where a user is present. Judge each grant by its type, not its name, because Mail Send as an application permission is critical. An application permission reaches across the whole tenant. And removing a permission from the app doesn't revoke the grant, so revoke it on the enterprise app too. Second, directory roles. No standing privileged role unless the record justifies it. A privileged service principal is a control-plane asset. Third, Azure roles, scoped to the one resource a workload uses. Fourth, custom security attributes, so Conditional Access can pick apps by fact. Fifth, workload Conditional Access, with real limits. Block is the only control. It covers only single-tenant apps, never managed identities, and only when each one is assigned directly. And new grants go through the tiered approval.

title: G4 in code: sweep the grants, ring the policies
say: The workbook's seventh chapter sweeps every grant. It reads app roles, delegated grants, directory roles and Azure roles for each service principal. On the fictional estate it finds eleven service principals and twenty grants, with seven findings. Three can grant themselves more, or hold an admin role, so they go to the Privileged Access plan instead. The plan has three writes: two app role removals and one narrowed grant. Each removal goes through the resource, never the app, and nothing is sent until a reviewer approves the plan's hash. The eighth chapter keeps the two workload policies as reviewed files, one per ring. Every policy is created in report-only mode. Then it reads the sign-ins. Ring one is ready. Ring two isn't, because one workload signed in from outside its known networks. Enforcement waits for the CISO's decision and a reviewed sign-in summary.

title: G4: requirement, evidence, availability, rollback
say: On the federal side, least privilege and the review of privileged accounts call for the kit runs, with a justification for every high grant, and the results of the PIM access reviews. CISA's baseline requires that only administrators register apps, that user consent is restricted, and that an admin consent workflow is in place, so keep the ScubaGear report. To validate, run three kit checks. One lists every high-privilege grant, and each must be justified or removed. One lists single-tenant apps outside a directly assigned policy, and no Tier 1 app may be on it. One looks for managed identities with broad Azure roles. Workload ID Premium is available in Azure Government through the account manager, but its free trial isn't. Without Premium, existing policies keep working but can't be edited. To roll back, set the policy back to report-only, and restore a removed grant through approval.

title: G5: build the target, run in parallel, then disable
say: Conversion follows Book 02's fourth phase. It takes six to eight weeks, and the order is a managed identity first, then a federated credential, then a certificate. Step one builds the target. A federated credential must be tested with a real token exchange. Step two names two human owners and a rotation schedule. Step three runs old and new side by side for thirty days. The application uses the new identity, and the old account stays enabled. Watch the new identity's sign-ins in Entra, and the old account's logons on the domain controllers. Step four disables the old account, but never deletes it. An Active Directory account moves to a holding container. A secret is removed only after the new credential has carried real traffic. Step five records the result: the target, the date, and the disabled object's ID.

title: G5 in code: test the exchange, plan the Kerberos moves
say: A federated credential with the wrong subject is created without any error. It fails only later, when the token exchange runs. So the workbook's fifth chapter tests every exchange before cutover, against a fake token endpoint. Here two of six tests fail. One credential copied a sample's issuer with a trailing slash, and wrote Production with a capital P. Another copied an audience with a leading space. The conversion records track each parallel run. One has run forty days cleanly, and its owner approved, so it's the one disable in the plan. Another is on day fifteen. A third still signed in with its old secret eight weeks after cutover. The sixth chapter plans the Kerberos accounts. It creates group managed service accounts, completes one migration, and builds the island list of accounts that stay, each with an owner and an end date.

title: G5: requirement, evidence, availability, rollback
say: On the federal side, authenticator management calls for the kit runs on expiring secrets and secret use, the app management policy export, and the rotation calendar. Service identification calls for each workload's permission grants and its sign-in log, which also shows the parallel run. Book 02 adds three tests: no stored secrets where possible, no outage during the run, and workload policies enforced. To validate, one kit check confirms no high-risk account still has a password that never expires. Another confirms the converted apps no longer hold secrets. Creating a federated credential and reading sign-ins work in the US Government clouds. A delegated managed service account needs Windows Server 2025. Until an account can move, it stays on the Kerberos island, with an owner and an end date. To roll back, re-enable the old account and revert the app. That stays possible until the account is deleted.

title: G6: owner change, orphans and owner reviews
say: A service account's events come from its owning system and from credential expiry, not from HR. The one exception is the sponsor. When an owner leaves or changes roles, the transfer starts at least ten business days ahead. Make it a step in that person's HR mover and leaver workflows, so nobody has to remember it. An app with no named owner is an orphan. It becomes Tier 1, the governance office takes it over, and there are thirty days to find an owner or start retiring it. On day thirty-one, access is suspended. An AI agent is disabled as soon as the finding is confirmed, because an agent can act. Inactivity is a second orphan signal, from a preview report of each service principal's last sign-in. And owners review their app's permissions every quarter, with at least two owners per app where possible.

title: G6: disable first, then delete
say: Retirement always disables first, so nothing breaks silently, and deletes later. The mechanics differ by type. An Active Directory account is disabled, and its service principal names are removed only after the observation period. An app registration is deactivated. New tokens stop at once, but tokens already issued stay valid until they expire. A deleted app can be restored for thirty days. A service principal is blocked from signing in to this tenant. If it's deleted and restored, its Conditional Access policies don't come back. A managed identity loses its role assignments first, and once deleted, it can't be recovered. An agent can be disabled by its sponsor, but not re-enabled. Deleting a blueprint removes its agents too. Every deactivation shows in the audit log. File that entry with the decision.

title: G6 in code: drift, the review cycle, the evidence chain
say: The workbook's tenth chapter turns this gate into a scheduled run. Each run compares every identity with a baseline that someone approved by its hash. On the second fixture day it finds seven ownerless orphan candidates, and two apps unused for over ninety days. It finds three accounts whose password never expires, and three credentials added outside the pipeline. A credential counts as the pipeline's only when two separate records agree. The review check finds an app whose last owner review was in May, too long ago. Then each run is packaged with a checksum for every file, chained to the day before. So a swapped package or a missing day shows up as a break. The period report is what the ISSO receives. Here the chain is unbroken, but the period isn't complete. Orphans and passwords that never expire are still open.

title: G6: requirement, evidence, availability, rollback
say: On the federal side, account management calls for the identity record, the owner-change and decommission tickets, and the kit runs for owners and agent sponsors. Identifier management calls for a record keyed by object ID, never reused. Audit controls call for the logs routed out of Entra ID, including every credential added and every deactivation. To validate, run the owner and expiry checks every week. A new app with fewer than two owners opens a ticket that week. No agent may go past ten business days without a confirmed sponsor. An optional preview check lists service principals idle for ninety days. Then run one test owner change and one test decommission, end to end. The sign-in activity report is listed only for the commercial service, so GCC has it, and GCC High doesn't. To roll back, reactivate, or restore within thirty days and re-create the Conditional Access assignments.

title: SQL Server: the engine, the instance, the applications
say: SQL Server follows the same logic, with three kinds of principal. The engine's service account works only while Active Directory is in charge. Azure Arc doesn't replace it. It only changes what Entra ID and Azure see. The instance's own Entra identity is a managed identity on SQL Server 2025, with no credential at all. On SQL Server 2022 it's an app registration with a Key Vault certificate, which needs a named renewal owner. Application logins move from SQL passwords to Entra logins: a managed identity first, then a certificate, and a secret only as a documented exception. And the same thirty-day parallel run applies. Two dangers stand out. A renewed certificate that nobody uploaded fails at expiry, so automate the upload. And on an Arc server, every allowed process presents the same identity, so treat one login per server as the unit of attribution.

title: AI agents: sponsors, blueprints and gated creation
say: AI agents follow this guide, with a few additions from Book 17. Every agent needs a sponsor when it's created. The blueprint holds the credentials, so one action on the blueprint reaches every agent made from it. Ordinary users can't create blueprints, and a production handshake comes before any agent goes live. No production blueprint holds a secret, and every API key is recorded as an exception. Access comes through packages with end dates, so a sponsor who does nothing lets access expire. The agent platform has been generally available since April 2026, with a partial subset in GCC. Agent Conditional Access is still in preview. The workbook's ninth chapter checks all of this, and here it finds twenty-two findings, four of them top priority. For GCC High and DoD, Microsoft has published nothing, so govern the service principals the agents run as.

title: Evidence and rollback across the track
say: Across the whole track, the evidence covers account management, least privilege, identifiers, authenticators, service identification and audit. It's the record, the tickets, the kit runs with their justifications, the access review results, the policy export, and the logs. Two CISA items sit across the track. ScubaGear also checks that apps have no passwords, and that credential lifetimes are capped. And it marks blocking risky AI agents as required, though CISA's own list didn't include it in late October. So record it now, and enforce it when agent risk is generally available in your cloud. Run the checks on the monitoring cadence, and file each run with its date, tenant and check version. Rollback is defined for every step. Part 1's steps roll back by re-deciding, or by an exception with an end date. Least privilege goes back to report-only. Conversion re-enables the old account. And decommissioning reactivates, or restores within thirty days.

title: The dangers to keep in view, and where to go next
say: Keep five dangers in view. Every app owner can add a credential and act as the app, so keep owners to the two people who configure it. Disabled isn't revoked, because issued tokens stay valid, so in an incident, also remove the credentials. A privileged service principal is a control-plane asset, not an ordinary app. Workload Conditional Access silently skips managed identities, multitenant apps, and anything assigned through a group. And by default, whoever builds an agent becomes its sponsor, so close blueprint creation and set the sponsor on purpose. Where to go next: Part 1 covers inventory, decisions and credential rules. The developer workbook, Building Non-Person Identity, has chapters five to ten for these gates, each with its labs. The Labs page lists them all. A person leaves and HR tells you. A service account's owner leaves and nothing tells you. These gates build the record that does.
